0.title: Training Up Children in the Fear of the Lord
0.overview:
Children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward (Ps 127:3). This is not sentimental — it is theological. Children are not our possessions, our projects, or our legacy. They are God's gift, entrusted to parents for a season, to be raised in the knowledge of the One who made them and loves them more than any parent ever could.

Christian parenting is the most significant discipleship task most believers will ever undertake. The average parent has more sustained, intimate influence over their children than any pastor, teacher, or mentor ever will. What happens in the home — in the ordinary rhythms of eating, sleeping, playing, arguing, forgiving, reading, praying, and living — shapes the child's understanding of God, of themselves, of love, of justice, and of what it means to be human more profoundly than almost any other force in their formation.

This is both an extraordinary privilege and a sobering responsibility. The parent who grasps it will not be paralysed by anxiety about getting everything right — they will be driven to their knees, to the Word, and to the community of the church, knowing that the task is too large for any single parent and that the God who gave the children has promised his presence in the raising of them.

Six units: (1) Children as Gift and Stewardship; (2) The Shema — comprehensive discipleship in the home; (3) Discipline and Grace — the gospel shape of correction; (4) The Father Heart of God — parenting from the overflow; (5) Prodigals and Difficult Seasons; (6) Releasing and Entrusting — the long view of parenting.

1.title: Children as Gift and Stewardship
1.overview:
Before we can parent well, we need to understand what children are. They are not blank slates waiting to be filled with the parents' values. They are not extensions of the parents' identity, instruments of the parents' ambitions, or sources of the parents' meaning. They are image-bearers — made in the likeness of God, with their own personhood, their own soul, their own relationship with God that no parent can substitute for or engineer.

This has enormous practical implications. The parent who treats their child as a project — something to be shaped, improved, and displayed — will produce either a performance-driven child who has learned to perform for approval, or a rebellious child who has discovered that authentic selfhood requires distance from the parent's agenda. The parent who treats their child as a person — made in God's image, loved by God, entrusted to them for a season — will parent with a different posture: not controlling but cultivating, not performing but serving, not owning but stearding.

Psalm 127 places children in a specifically theological context: unless the LORD builds the house, the parents labour in vain. The most diligent, intentional, theologically informed parenting is ultimately dependent on the sovereign grace of the God who saves. Parents plant and water — God gives the growth (1 Cor 3:6–7). This does not make parenting passive; it makes it prayerful. And it releases parents from the crushing burden of believing that their child's spiritual outcome depends entirely on them.
1.theology:
The image of God in children: Every child, from conception, bears the image of God — which means every child has irreducible dignity, personhood, and moral significance. This is why the Scriptures treat children as full human beings rather than apprentice humans. The child's questions, fears, joys, and worship are not preliminary sketches of adult experience — they are the real thing, offered by a real person to the real God. Jesus received children that his disciples tried to turn away (Mark 10:13–16) and declared that the kingdom belongs to such as these.

Stewardship, not ownership: The legal language of ancient Israel included the concept that children ultimately belonged to God, not to their parents. They were circumcised as a sign of the covenant that preceded their birth; they were dedicated to God (as Samuel was, 1 Sam 1:28); they were raised within the covenant community, not merely within the nuclear family. This communal, covenantal context for child-raising is a corrective to the hyper-individualistic parenting culture of the contemporary West, in which parents bear the full weight of child-formation alone.

The limits of parental influence: Proverbs 22:6 — "Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it" — is a promise of wisdom, not an iron guarantee. Like all Proverbs, it states the general principle: faithful formation produces lasting fruit. But it does not mean that a faithfully raised child will never wander, or that a prodigal child is evidence of failed parenting. God is the ultimate parent of his people, and his children still wander. Parental faithfulness is our responsibility; the child's response is their own, and ultimately God's to secure.
1.examples:
Hannah's prayer and dedication: Hannah prayed for a son with such intensity that Eli thought she was drunk. When God gave her Samuel, she brought him to the house of the LORD and dedicated him: "I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD" (1 Sam 1:28). This is the posture of the Christian parent: the child is received as a gift and returned to the Giver. Hannah did not cease to be Samuel's mother — she made his robe and brought it to him each year (1 Sam 2:19). But she held him with an open hand, knowing that he was God's first and hers only in trust.

Deuteronomy as parenting curriculum: Moses addressed Deuteronomy not just to adults but to the covenant community as a whole, including children who were explicitly summoned to hear the law (Deut 31:12). The entire book is framed around transmission: these words are to be taught to your children and your grandchildren (Deut 4:9). The Scriptures were designed for intergenerational transmission — not from expert to novice but from parent to child, in the home, in daily life, in the ordinary rhythms of covenant community.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, children are a heritage from the LORD, the fruit of the womb a reward. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The word heritage (nahalah) is the word used for the land of Canaan — the inheritance God gave his people as a covenantal gift. Children are in the same category: a covenantal gift, something given by God for the family's blessing and for his purposes in the world. The word reward (sakar) does not imply that children are earned — it describes the joy and the good that they bring. This reframes the entirely contemporary question of whether to have children: the biblical framework is not primarily about lifestyle calculation but about receiving or declining a divine gift.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Jesus saw it, he was indignant and said to them, "Let the children come to me; do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of God." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus was indignant — a strong word — when his disciples tried to turn the children away. Children are not peripheral to the kingdom; they are its paradigm. The kingdom of God belongs to such as these — not because children are innocent (they are not) but because they are small, dependent, non-achieving, and receive freely. The posture of the child — open-handed, trusting, un-self-sufficient — is the posture of every kingdom citizen. The parent who teaches their child to come to Jesus is teaching them the most important thing they will ever learn.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I have lent him to the LORD. As long as he lives, he is lent to the LORD. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Hannah's theology of parenthood in one sentence: the child is lent. She received him as a gift; she returns him to the Giver; she will receive him back in a different form throughout his life. This is the open-handed posture that Christian parenting requires — not detachment (Hannah wept, prayed, and made his robe) but surrender. The parent who holds their child with a clenched fist will either crush the child or be crushed by the child's choices. The parent who holds them with an open hand, continually offering them back to God, is freed from the anxiety of control and grounded in the peace of trust.

verseByVerse.quote: We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD, and his might, and the wonders that he has done. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Generational transmission is the explicit design of Psalm 78 — God's mighty deeds are to move from generation to generation, from parents to children to grandchildren, in an unbroken chain of testimony. The parent who tells their children what God has done — in Scripture, in history, and in their own life — is not merely providing religious education; they are participating in the great intergenerational project of keeping the memory of God's faithfulness alive in the earth. The child who grows up hearing stories of God's faithfulness has a very different foundation for faith than the child who grows up hearing stories of human achievement.

2.title: The Shema: Comprehensive Discipleship in the Home
2.overview:
The most important passage in the Bible for Christian parenting is not in the New Testament — it is Deuteronomy 6:4–9, the Shema. "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one. You shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might." And then the parenting instruction: "And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise."

The Shema gives us the curriculum (the great commandment — love God with everything), the method (talk of them diligently), and the classroom (every moment of ordinary life — sitting, walking, lying down, rising). This is not a programme. It is a posture — a way of inhabiting daily life with theological intentionality, so that every moment becomes an occasion for the child to encounter the living God through the medium of the parent's life and words.

The key phrase is "these words shall be on your heart" — the instruction begins with the parent's own devotion to God, not with a technique for teaching children. You cannot transmit what you do not possess. The parent who is themselves captivated by God — who prays, reads Scripture, meditates, and lives with the love of God as their deepest motivation — will find that their children catch what they carry, even before the formal teaching begins. Discipleship in the home is more caught than taught.
2.theology:
The home as primary discipleship context: In ancient Israel, the family was the primary unit of religious education — not the synagogue, not the school, not the professional teacher. The father was the family priest (Gen 18:19), responsible for teaching the faith to his household. This does not diminish the role of the gathered community (the church) in Christian formation — but it does establish the family as the primary arena in which faith is transmitted, practiced, and embodied. The church strengthens and supports what the home does; the home cannot be outsourced to the church.

Caught and taught: The Shema's method is not primarily classroom instruction — it is immersive life. The child who sees their parent pray with genuine fervour, who hears their parent speak of God with genuine love, who observes their parent handle failure and disappointment with genuine trust — this child is learning the faith in the most powerful way possible. Formal instruction (Bible stories, catechism, family devotions) is valuable and commanded; but it is most powerful when it is set within a life that gives it flesh.

The heart as the target: The Shema's goal is not behavioural compliance but heart devotion — love for God with all the heart, soul, and might. The parent whose goal is obedient behaviour will produce either a genuinely compliant child (who has learned to conform outwardly) or a rebellious child (who has detected that the real goal is control, not love). The parent whose goal is love for God will parent differently — seeking to make God attractive, to demonstrate his goodness, to create experiences of his love, so that the child's heart is drawn to him rather than driven to him.
2.examples:
Timothy's formation: Paul writes to Timothy that he has been acquainted with the sacred writings since childhood (2 Tim 3:15) and that this knowledge came through his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice (2 Tim 1:5). Three generations of women transmitting faith — the grandmother, the mother, the result: one of Paul's most trusted co-workers. This is the Shema working across generations: faith caught and taught, embodied and communicated, received and then given again.

Family worship: The Puritan tradition developed the practice of family worship — a daily gathering of the household for Scripture reading, prayer, and singing — as the most direct application of the Shema's command. Richard Baxter, the great Puritan pastor, argued that the reformation of the church begins in the reformation of the home. The family that prays together — even imperfectly, even briefly, even in seasons of resistance — is building the patterns of devotion that will sustain faith across a lifetime.

verseByVerse.quote: And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart. You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Four moments: sitting, walking, lying down, rising — the whole arc of daily life. The instruction is not to add a religious programme to the daily schedule but to make the whole daily schedule a religious programme. The mealtime conversation, the bedtime prayer, the car journey, the morning routine — all are opportunities for the faith to be spoken, demonstrated, and embedded. This is discipleship by immersion, and it is far more powerful than any formal curriculum, because it trains the child's imagination and instincts as well as their mind.

verseByVerse.quote: And how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: From childhood — the Greek word is brephos, meaning infancy. Timothy was acquainted with the sacred writings from infancy. This was not academic acquaintance — it was the acquaintance of one who has heard the stories, prayed the prayers, and lived within the world that Scripture describes. The sacred writings that make wise for salvation are not merely information to be downloaded — they are a world to be inhabited from the earliest possible age. The parent who reads Scripture to their children before the children can understand every word is doing something profound: they are creating the linguistic and imaginative world within which the child will eventually make sense of the gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This proverb is both a promise and a principle. The word translated train (chanak) is related to the word for the dedication of a building — it suggests an inaugural, foundational act of orientation. The way he should go may also be rendered the way suited to him — the direction of the child's own particular bent. The proverb does not promise that every faithfully raised child will never wander; it states the wisdom principle that early formation has lasting effects. The parent who is faithful in early formation plants seeds that may lie dormant for decades before germinating. Some of the most powerful testimonies to parental faithfulness come from prodigals who, years later, returned to what they were taught.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two commands, inseparable. Do not provoke — do not exasperate by unreasonable demands, inconsistency, favouritism, harshness, or the crushing of the child's personhood. And bring up in discipline and instruction — paideia (the Greek word for the comprehensive formation of a person) and nouthesia (the admonishing, instructive counsel that shapes the mind and will). The two commands are held in tension: the parent who only disciplines without relationship provokes; the parent who only nurtures without discipline fails to instruct. The gospel parent does both — creating the relationship of trust within which correction is received rather than resented.

3.title: Discipline and Grace: The Gospel Shape of Correction
3.overview:
Few areas of Christian parenting generate more confusion, controversy, or anxiety than discipline. The biblical teaching on discipline is clear but not simple — it requires wisdom, love, and a deep understanding of both the child's heart and the gospel's shape. The parent who applies biblical discipline without gospel grace will produce moralism and resentment. The parent who applies gospel grace without biblical discipline will produce a child who has never encountered the serious love of God that Hebrews 12 describes.

The Bible's view of discipline is rooted in a theology of love. Hebrews 12:5–11 is the key text: God disciplines those he loves, as a father disciplines the son in whom he delights. Discipline is not punishment administered by an angry authority — it is the loving formation offered by a Father who is entirely committed to his child's good, even when that good requires pain. The child who is never corrected, never experience the loving consequences of wrong choices, never encounters the firm but kind hand of authority is a child who has not received the full love of a good father.

The goal of all discipline is not compliance but character — not a child who obeys to avoid punishment but a child who has internalised the values and virtues that make for a good human life. This long-term goal requires that discipline be consistently connected to relationship: the child must know that correction comes from love, not from anger or rejection; that the parent's approval is not conditional on performance; and that the gospel of forgiveness applies within the family as surely as it applies to the world outside.
3.theology:
The theology of Hebrews 12: God disciplines his children for their good — that we may share in his holiness (Heb 12:10). The purpose of discipline is not punishment (the payment of a debt) but formation (the development of holiness). This is the crucial distinction: punishment looks backward, to what was done; discipline looks forward, to what the person is becoming. The parent who disciplines for formation rather than punishment will discipline differently — with clarity about the behaviour, compassion for the child's heart, consistency in application, and confidence in the goal.

The rod passages: Proverbs references the rod of discipline (Prov 13:24, 22:15, 23:13–14, 29:15) in a way that has generated significant debate. Most Reformed scholars understand these texts to commend appropriate physical correction (spanking) as one tool among many, used with controlled restraint, connected to relationship, and age-appropriate. The parent who uses physical discipline carelessly, angrily, or excessively has left behind the biblical pattern and moved into harm. The parent who abandons all correction as harmful has also left behind the biblical pattern and moved into a permissiveness that Proverbs calls hatred of the child (Prov 13:24).

Grace in discipline: Every act of parental discipline is an opportunity to preach the gospel. When a child is corrected, they experience something of what God's law does — it shows that what they did was wrong, that wrong has consequences, and that relationship is at stake. When the correction is followed by forgiveness, reassurance of love, and restoration of relationship, the child experiences something of what the gospel does. The family that disciplines and forgives, corrects and restores, is doing applied soteriology at the kitchen table.
3.examples:
Eli's failure: Eli the priest had sons who were wicked (1 Sam 2:12) and he did not restrain them (1 Sam 3:13). God's judgment on Eli was severe — not because he was himself wicked but because he honoured his sons above God (1 Sam 2:29) and failed to exercise the loving authority that his fatherhood required. The parent who refuses to discipline out of a desire to be liked by their children, or out of an inability to bear their displeasure, has made the same error as Eli: they have placed the child's momentary comfort above the child's long-term formation.

Tedd Tripp's shepherding model: Tedd Tripp's Shepherding a Child's Heart applies the biblical framework of the heart to discipline: discipline that only addresses behaviour without addressing the heart is like cutting a weed at ground level — the root remains. The parent's goal is to understand what the child's heart was doing in the wrong behaviour (what did they want? what were they afraid of? what were they trying to control?) and to address that, as well as the behaviour. This requires both correction and conversation — and a genuine interest in the child as a person rather than a problem to be solved.

verseByVerse.quote: For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment all discipline seems painful rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained by it. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two time horizons: the moment (painful) and the later (peaceful fruit of righteousness). The parent who disciplines only attends to the moment — the child's tears, the resistance, the difficulty of the confrontation. The parent who disciplines wisely keeps the later in view: this is forming something. The painful moment is the price of the future fruit. This is how God parents: for our good, that we may share his holiness. The parent who grasps this is freed from the guilt of causing short-term pain in the service of long-term formation.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever spares the rod hates his son, but he who loves him is diligent to discipline him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Proverbs makes the connection explicit: love disciplines. The parent who cannot bear to correct, who is more committed to the child's momentary happiness than to their formation, is — in Proverbs' sharp language — a parent who hates their child. Not in intention but in effect: the undisciplined child is being denied one of the fundamental forms of parental love. The connection between love and discipline is not a paradox but a theological necessity — the God who loves absolutely also disciplines consistently (Heb 12:6), and the parent made in his image is called to the same combination.

verseByVerse.quote: Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's warning to fathers in Colossians is even simpler than in Ephesians — one command, one consequence: do not provoke, lest they become discouraged. The word discouraged (athumeo) means to lose heart, to become spiritless. The child who is chronically criticised, never affirmed, held to unreachable standards, or corrected in anger rather than love eventually loses heart — gives up trying, withdraws, or rebels. The father who provokes has damaged the relationship within which all his instruction and discipline must operate. Relationship is the medium through which all parental formation travels.

verseByVerse.quote: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The father in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son is the model of the parent who disciplines through consequence (he let the son go), watches with longing (he saw him while he was still far off), runs without hesitation (he did not wait for the apology to be complete), and restores without qualification (the best robe, the ring, the feast). This is the gospel shape of parental love: it allows the painful consequence of wrong choices, it watches with undiminished love, and it runs to restore when the child turns. Every Christian parent is called to embody this — toward their own children, and in so doing, to make the Father's love visible.

4.title: The Father Heart of God: Parenting from the Overflow
4.overview:
The most important thing a Christian parent can do for their child is to know God as Father. Not merely to know the doctrine of divine fatherhood — to know the living God who runs to prodigals, who numbers the hairs of his children's heads, who neither slumbers nor sleeps as he watches over them, who works all things together for their good, who disciplines them for their holiness, and who has prepared an eternal home for them. The parent who knows this God parents from the overflow of that knowledge.

The parent who does not know God as Father — who relates to God primarily through duty, guilt, or performance anxiety — will almost inevitably parent their children from the same posture: demanding performance, dispensing approval conditionally, maintaining relationship through the child's compliance. This is not a personality fault; it is a theological deficit. The cure is not better parenting techniques but a deeper experience of the Father's love.

Paul prays that the Ephesians would know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Eph 3:19) — because only the person who has been flooded with that love has enough to give it away lavishly. The parent who has been loved well by God can love their child lavishly — not because they are naturally patient and generous but because they are drawing from a source that does not run dry. This is what it means to parent from the overflow: not to manufacture love from personal virtue but to receive it from God and pass it on.
4.theology:
God as the perfect Father: Jesus teaches us to pray "Our Father" — the most intimate and audacious form of address available to the creature before the Creator. The Father who is addressed in the Lord's Prayer is the model for all human fatherhood (Eph 3:14–15 — from the Father every family in heaven and earth is named). Every good human father is a dim reflection of the perfect Father; every failure of human fatherhood is an occasion to point children beyond the imperfect father to the perfect one. The parent who acknowledges their failures to their children — and points them to the Father who never fails — is doing something profoundly theological.

The Holy Spirit and parenting: The fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Gal 5:22–23) — is simultaneously a description of the perfect parent and an indication of where parental virtue comes from. The parent who is patient with their child is not drawing on a reservoir of natural patience — they are manifesting the fruit of the Spirit that the Spirit is producing in them. This means that the prayer for parental virtue is a prayer for the Spirit's fruit: "Lord, give me patience with my child" is a prayer the Spirit delights to answer.

Parenting as calling, not identity: The parent who has made parenting their primary identity — whose sense of worth rises and falls with their children's performance and choices — has made parenting an idol. The consequences are painful: anxious, over-involved parenting that smothers the child; devastating collapse when the child makes poor choices; inability to release the child into adulthood. The parent whose identity is in Christ — not in their parenting success — can parent with both intensity and freedom: intense because they love the child deeply, free because their worth does not depend on the outcome.
4.examples:
The prodigal's father: Luke 15's father is the Bible's most detailed portrait of the Father heart of God, and therefore of the parenting heart that Christians are called to embody. He lets the son go — he does not chain him to duty. He watches — he does not forget or harden his heart. He runs — he does not stand on dignity or wait for sufficient repentance. He restores lavishly — he does not impose a probationary period. This is extravagant, undignified, unconditional love. The parent who prays to love like this, and who asks God to form this love in them by his Spirit, is praying a prayer that the Father — who runs to his own prodigals — is delighted to answer.

J.I. Packer on knowing God as Father: Packer, in Knowing God, identifies the knowledge of God as Father as the highest privilege of the Christian life — the summit of the gospel's gifts. "What is a Christian? The richest answer I know is that a Christian is one who has God as Father." The parent who has this richness — who knows, not merely believes, that God is their Father — has a resource for parenting that no technique, curriculum, or method can supply. They have access to the One from whom every family is named.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I bow my knees before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Every family — in heaven and on earth — derives its name, its meaning, and its pattern from the Father. Human fatherhood and motherhood are not accidental biological facts — they are reflections of the nature of God himself. The parent who understands this is humbled (they are a dim reflection of the original) and encouraged (the original is available to them, and his Spirit will supply what their nature lacks). The family is not a human invention that God has chosen to bless; it is a divine institution that reflects something essential about who God is.

verseByVerse.quote: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Read this list as a description of the parent their child needs: loving, joyful, at peace, patient, kind, good, faithful, gentle, self-controlled. Now ask: where does this come from? Not from natural virtue, not from parenting courses, not from sufficient sleep (though that helps). It comes from the Spirit. The parent who is being transformed by the Spirit is becoming the parent their child needs — not perfectly, not immediately, but progressively. The most important thing a parent can do for their children is grow in the Spirit themselves. Their spiritual health is their children's greatest inheritance.

verseByVerse.quote: For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Spirit of adoption — the Spirit who gives us the intimate cry of "Abba, Father" — is the Spirit who enables the Christian to know God as Father in their bones, not merely in their theology. The parent who cries Abba in genuine intimacy, who brings their parenting fears and failures and joys to the Father with the freedom of an adopted child — this parent has a relationship that sustains the whole enterprise of raising children. They do not parent alone; they parent from within the Father's embrace.

verseByVerse.quote: Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God uses the image of nursing-mother love to describe his own love for his people — the most instinctive, visceral, self-giving love in human experience. And then he exceeds it: even a nursing mother might forget, but he will not. This is the love from which all human parental love derives its pattern and its power. The parent who loves their child with fierce, instinctive, self-giving love is reflecting God's own love — and the child who knows that God loves them even more than their parent does has found a security that no human love, however devoted, can fully provide.

5.title: Prodigals and Difficult Seasons
5.overview:
Every generation of Christian parents has produced prodigals. Children who were raised in the faith, prayed for, taught the Scriptures, brought to worship, and saturated with the gospel — who have nonetheless walked away. Children who are struggling with addictions, broken relationships, confusion about identity, or a hard-heartedness toward God that breaks their parents' hearts. This is not a new problem; it is the oldest problem — the problem of human freedom and the mystery of God's sovereignty.

The parent of a prodigal carries a particular grief that is unlike almost any other: the grief of watching someone you love choose a path you know leads to harm, of being unable to prevent it, of praying without visible answer, of loving a person who may not want your love. This grief is real and it is legitimate. Jesus wept. The father in the parable watched and waited. Paul wrote from prison about churches that had disappointed him. The Bible does not pretend that faithful parenting always produces faithful children, and it does not require the parent of a prodigal to pretend otherwise.

The parent of a prodigal needs three things: first, the theological framework that releases them from the crushing burden of believing the outcome is entirely their fault; second, the practical wisdom about how to maintain relationship with a child who has made choices they cannot affirm; third, the community of the church to sustain them in prayer and fellowship through the long and often invisible work of waiting. None of these three needs can be met by a parenting technique. They require the gospel, wisdom, and the body of Christ.
5.theology:
God's sovereignty and human freedom: The parent of a prodigal inevitably wrestles with the relationship between God's sovereignty and their child's choices. Did God ordain this? Could he have prevented it? Reformed theology does not flinch from the question: God is sovereign over all things, including the choices of prodigal children. But his sovereignty does not make the choices unchosen — the prodigal is genuinely choosing. Both are true, and the tension between them is one that the parent must hold without resolution in this life. The consolation is this: the God who is sovereign over all things loves the prodigal more than the parent does, and he has not given up.

The ministry of waiting: Luke 15:20 — "while he was still a long way off, his father saw him" — implies that the father was watching. He was not passive in his waiting; he was attentive, positioned, ready. The parent of a prodigal is called to the ministry of watching and waiting: praying persistently, keeping the relationship open, communicating love without condoning choices, and believing in the possibility of return. This is not passive endurance — it is active faith, the faith that keeps the light on and the door unlocked.

When to speak and when to be silent: One of the hardest practical questions for the parent of a prodigal is when to speak the truth about their child's choices and when to remain silent. The pattern of the father in Luke 15 is instructive: he did not lecture the departing son, he did not plead or bargain, he allowed the consequences of the son's choices to do their work — and he was ready and joyful when the son returned. This is not indifference; it is respect for the child's personhood and trust in God's ability to speak to the child's heart without the parent's constant intervention.
5.examples:
Augustine and Monica: Monica prayed for her wayward son Augustine for seventeen years — through his concubinage, his intellectual wandering, his Manichaeism. She followed him to Italy when he deceived her and sailed without her. She prayed, she wept, she persisted. The bishop Ambrose told her: "It is impossible that the son of such tears should perish." Augustine's Confessions are, among other things, a tribute to a mother's persistent prayer. The prodigal's return came — the most significant intellectual and theological conversion in church history. Monica's prayer was part of it.

The distant father: Paul Tripp observes that many Christian parents respond to a prodigal child by withdrawing — withdrawing emotionally (to protect themselves), withdrawing relationally (to punish the child's choices), or withdrawing theologically (deciding that the child is beyond grace). The father in Luke 15 did none of these things. He kept watching. He kept the relationship open. He ran when the son returned. The parent who remains relationally present to their prodigal — who loves without approving, who maintains contact without endorsing choices — is keeping the path of return available. And the God who ran to his own prodigals will, in his time, run to theirs.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he came to himself, he said, "How many of my father's hired servants have more than enough bread, but I perish here with hunger! I will arise and go to my father." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The prodigal "came to himself" — came back to reality, came back to sanity, came back to the truth about where he was and who his father was. This moment of clarity was not produced by his father's lecturing or manipulation — it was produced by his circumstances and, the Christian would say, by the Spirit. The parent of a prodigal cannot engineer this moment; they can pray for it, remain present for it, and be ready with open arms when it comes. The father's role in Luke 15 during the prodigal's absence is almost invisible — he watched, he waited, he prayed. And then he ran.

verseByVerse.quote: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jeremiah wrote these words in the rubble of Jerusalem, after everything had been destroyed. The parent of a prodigal knows something of Jeremiah's devastation. These words are the parent's lifeline: the steadfast love does not cease. The mercies are new every morning — not depleted by last night's grief, not exhausted by years of unanswered prayer, not diminished by the child's persistent choices. New every morning. Great is your faithfulness — the parent who cannot see what God is doing can still affirm what God is. And the God who is faithful to his prodigal people is faithful to their prodigal children too.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor anything else in all creation, will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Nothing separates the prodigal from the love of God in Christ — not their choices, not their distance, not their time away. The parent who knows this has something to hold in the dark nights of praying for a child who has wandered: the love that pursues them is stronger than the choices that have led them away. The parent is not the last line of defence between the prodigal and destruction; God is. And God's love — which went to the cross for its objects — is more tenacious, more patient, and more resourceful than any human love could be.

verseByVerse.quote: Casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The parental anxiety of a prodigal season is real and heavy. Peter's command is both an instruction and a permission: cast all of it on God — the fear for the child's safety, the grief of watching them choose harm, the confusion about what to say and what not to say, the longing for return. All of it. The word cast (epiripsantes) is used for throwing something — not a gentle setting down but a deliberate, active transfer. God can bear the weight that is crushing you. And the motivation is not a principle but a person: he cares for you. The God who cares for the anxious parent cares equally for the wandering child.

6.title: Releasing and Entrusting: The Long View of Parenting
6.overview:
The goal of Christian parenting is not to produce a child who needs their parent forever. It is to raise a person who is so deeply rooted in God — so formed by faith, so established in character, so connected to the community of the church — that they can walk with him faithfully through the whole of their independent life. The parent who has done this well has worked themselves out of the primary-discipleship role — and the measure of their success is not that the child never leaves but that when they leave, they are ready.

This releasing is one of the most emotionally demanding things parents face — and one of the most theologically important. The parent who cannot release their child is holding onto something that was always God's, imposing a dependence that was always meant to be temporary, and preventing the growth that can only happen in independence. The parent who releases with grace, with blessing, with prayer, and with the confidence that the God who has been faithful thus far will continue to be faithful — this parent is enacting the theology of Hannah, of Abraham, of every parent who has learned to hold their children with an open hand.

And then comes the long view: watching the adult child navigate their own faith, their own marriage, their own parenting. Praying across the distance. Offering wisdom when asked, releasing when not. Being the grandparent who prays for the next generation. Participating in the intergenerational work of the kingdom that Psalm 78 describes — a chain of testimony and trust stretching from grandparents to children to grandchildren, across the decades, until Christ returns.
6.theology:
Genesis 2:24 and leaving: The same verse that grounds the theology of marriage grounds the theology of releasing: a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife. The leaving is the child's act — but it requires the parent's blessing and release. The parent who has raised their child toward this leaving — who has been preparing them for independence throughout childhood, who has been gradually releasing authority and responsibility as maturity grows — will not be blindsided when the leaving comes. They will celebrate it, because it is the sign of work well done.

Abraham and Isaac: Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac (Gen 22) is the Bible's most extreme picture of releasing a child to God — and God's provision of the substitute ram is the assurance that the God who calls us to release our children has not abandoned them. He has received them. The parent who offers their child to God — in the ordinary sense of releasing their control, their agenda, and their anxiety — is participating in the pattern of Abraham. And the God who provided for Abraham's child will provide for theirs.

The long obedience: Eugene Peterson's phrase — a long obedience in the same direction — applies to parenting as much as to the Christian life in general. There is no parenting programme that produces the desired results in a month. The formation of a human being is the work of decades — consistent, faithful, unglamorous, daily. The parent who commits to the long obedience of faithful presence, daily prayer, consistent love, honest correction, and joyful celebration will look back at the end and see something that they could not see while they were doing it: the hand of God in the whole story.
6.examples:
Lois and Eunice: Two generations of women — grandmother and mother — whose faithful formation of Timothy produced one of the most significant gospel workers of the apostolic age. They did not live to see the full fruit of what they planted (Timothy was Paul's companion when 2 Timothy was written; they may well have been dead by then). The parent who plants seeds of faith in their children is planting some seeds they will see germinate in their lifetime and others they will not. The harvest belongs to God; the planting is their calling.

The blessing: The biblical tradition of parental blessing — Jacob blessing his sons (Gen 49), Moses blessing the tribes (Deut 33), Isaac blessing his sons (Gen 27–28) — is a powerful practice that many Christian families have lost. To bless a child — to speak specifically and intentionally about who they are, what gifts you see in them, what hope you have for their future, and what the hand of God has been doing in their life — is to do something profoundly formative. It is to say: I see you, I love you, I release you, and I trust the God who made you to complete what he has begun.

verseByVerse.quote: He established a testimony in Jacob and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers to teach to their children, that the next generation might know them, the children yet unborn, and arise and tell them to their children, so that they should set their hope in God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The vision is multigenerational: grandparents to parents to children to grandchildren, the testimony of God's faithfulness moving across the generations like a river. The parent who teaches their child is already thinking about their grandchildren — the children yet unborn who will need the same testimony. This long view transforms the daily work of parenting: every bedtime prayer, every dinner-table conversation about God, every honest moment of faith in front of the children, is a thread in a tapestry that will stretch across generations. The parent plants; the grandchildren may harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Do not lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The test of Abraham was a test of whether he would withhold his most treasured gift from God. The parent who fears God does not withhold their child — they offer them back to the One who gave them. This offering takes different forms: the offering of the infant in dedication, the offering of the teenager in prayer when the parent cannot control the outcome, the offering of the adult child when they make choices the parent would not have chosen. In every case, the act of not withholding — of releasing control and trusting God — is the act of parental faith.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am sure of this, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul's confidence in the Philippians is the Christian parent's confidence in their child: the One who began a good work will bring it to completion. The parent does not complete the work — they participate in a work that God began before the child was born and will finish on the day of Christ. This conviction is the parent's freedom from anxiety: the outcome is not in your hands. It is in the hands of the One who began it. Your calling is faithfulness; his calling is completion. Trust the Finisher — and rest in him.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD bless you and keep you; the LORD make his face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance upon you and give you peace. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Aaronic blessing — the oldest liturgical text in the world, still spoken over congregations and children — is the parent's benediction over the child they release. Bless and keep: may God's goodness be upon you and may his protection surround you. Shine his face: may the warmth of his presence be your light. Gracious: may his free, unearned favour be the ground you walk on. Peace: shalom — the comprehensive wellbeing of the person who is in right relationship with God and with the world. This is the parent's deepest prayer for the child they release. It is also the promise of the God who receives the child they offer.
